pages.text:
*Ama's Stall Ledger, Night 54. Bowls sold: 19. Sky Mall: open. Ama's mood: quiet.*

The streetlights flickered, and then the world turned white. Sky Mall had opened. The lights were so bright they washed out the red lanterns on our lane, making them look like faded fruit. I stood on the sidewalk, feeling small and dusty.

Auntie Ping ran over, her pom-pom headband bouncing. Her eyes were wide, reflecting the glass. "Look at that," she whispered. "Free bubble tea for the first thousand people. And the food court. Did you see the screens?"

She looked at me, really looked at me. "Lin, it looks exactly like the future."

I felt a cold spot open in my stomach. I reached into my jacket pocket and touched the folded paper where I had drawn my own plans for modernizing our stall. Clean lines. Digital menus. I had wanted this. I had wished for this. But standing there, in the cold, smelling only of damp pavement and distant exhaust, I did not want it at all.
pages.image: A girl in a green jacket and checked apron stands on a dark street looking up at a massive, brightly lit modern glass mall with white counters and glowing screens, while a woman with a pom-pom headband points excitedly at the building.

pages.text:
By seven o'clock, the lane had emptied out completely. It felt like a bathtub draining, the water pulling away fast until only the scum and the silence remained. We sold nineteen bowls that night. I wrote the number down, and the ink looked too black and too loud against the paper.

Uncle Feng’s griddle sat cold and silent. It did not hiss or sizzle, just resting there as a dark disc of metal under the harsh lights. Old Mr. Gao sat by his shrimp pond, talking to the water.

"Hello, shrimp," he said to an empty bowl. "Do you like jazz?"

He waited for an answer, but there was none. Then I saw him. Jun’s dad was walking through the mall’s glass doors, wearing a crisp white apron that did not match anything in this lane. He was carrying a tray of plates. He looked thin. He looked like he was walking in a dream that didn’t belong to him.
pages.image: An empty night market lane at night with closed stalls and plastic stools, an old man in a straw hat sitting alone by a dark water pond, and a man in a white apron carrying a tray walking away toward bright glass doors.

pages.text:
A car pulled up to the curb. The door opened, and Yi-Chen stepped out. She was wearing a pink puffy vest and holding a shiny paper bag that crinkled loudly in the quiet air. Her mother stood behind her, adjusting a scarf.

"It’s a shame, really," Yi-Chen said, looking at the dark stalls. "But I guess that’s how things are. The food court has everything in one place. So convenient."

She looked at me, waiting for me to agree. I wanted to agree. I wanted to say yes, it is convenient, it is clean, it is better. But the words that came out of my mouth were sharp and cold.

"The food court has everything," I said. "Except a grandmother."

Yi-Chen blinked. Her mouth opened slightly. For one second, I felt a hot spark of victory. Then the spark died, and I felt the cold of the street again.
pages.image: A girl in a pink puffy vest holding a shiny paper bag stands on a sidewalk talking to a girl in a green jacket and checked apron, with a woman in a scarf standing behind them in front of a dark, empty street stall.

pages.text:
Auntie Ping did not leave. She stood by her machine, the plastic cups stacked high and untouched, and for the first time in my life, I heard her silence. It was a very different kind of quiet than the pause between customers.

"Lin," she said softly. "They called me."

We did not turn around. Uncle Feng stopped wiping his hands on his apron, and Old Mr. Gao forgot to check his shrimp pond. The air felt heavy, like the moment before a rainstorm that never actually starts falling.

"They offered me a booth," Auntie Ping said. "Inside. With air conditioning. And the lights are always on."

She touched the top of her tea machine, her glittery nails brushing against the cold metal with a faint click. I looked at the steam rising from the vents, wondering if it would ever stop.

"I won't decide until after the Lantern Festival," she said. But she was not looking at us. She was looking at the machine, and her eyes seemed to belong to somebody else, somebody who had already packed her bags and left for a warmer room.
pages.image: A woman with glittery nails and a pom-pom headband stands beside a bubble tea machine, her hand resting on the metal, while a girl in a green jacket watches her with a worried expression in a dimly lit stall.

pages.text:
Ama did not speak, and she did not hum, which was the worst part. The silence from her was heavier than the traffic on the main road. She wiped the same table, the one by the window, three times in a row. She dried it, wiped it, and dried it again, her towel moving in small, tight circles.

The great pot was cold. I could see it. The steam had stopped rising, and the surface of the broth was still and dark, like a bowl of soup that had forgotten how to be hot.

I looked at the folded paper in my pocket. My plans. My modern stall. My clean lines. I realized, with a horror that made my knees feel like wet noodles, that I had not been dreaming of change. I had been dreaming of leaving. And now, the thing I had wished for was standing at the end of the lane, glowing, waiting for us to walk away.
pages.image: A small elderly woman with silver curls wipes a table at a night market stall, while a girl in a green jacket watches her with a sad and worried expression, a large cold pot of soup sitting still on the stove behind them.
